name: Mwera
catalog_citation: Harries, Lyndon. 1950. A Grammar of Mwera (Bantu Grammatical Archives 1). Johannesburg: Witwatersrand University Press. x+127 pp.
catalog_locator: Ch. I (Phonology), section 'Stress', p. 15 (Google Books search-inside snippets, page_id PA15, volume ids -J1kAAAAMAAJ and g0o0AQAAIAAJ, identical text); also …
catalog_quote: STRESS Stress, in Mwera, accompanied by length and a rising tone, is normally on the penultimate syllable. Each word in Mwera has one main stress, e.g.: ngakumumánya (I do not understand). When a word is increased in length by the addition of formative suffixes, the main stress moves forward to remain upon the penultimate syllable, e.g.: céma, ceméla, cemána, ceméya, cemilwe, etc. The suffixes -pe and -ga (or -je) do not always bring the stress forward. If the syllable taking the stress is long, it retains the stress even when the suffix is employed, e.g.: kundáwipe (early in the morning) nikaga ñne (if I come) ajéndeje (let him go! or, polite for, Go then!). Trisyllabic verbs have the stress on the ante-penultimate syllable in their simple forms, but the stress is penultimate with endings in verb conjugation, e.g.: kukágula (to follow) ... (he followed) kupyájila (to sweep) > kupyajili…

new_statements.rule_in_words: Each word has one main stress, which falls on the penultimate syllable and is realised with vowel length and a rising pitch; stress shifts rightward under suffixation so as to stay penultimate.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Harries mentions a 'secondary stress with trisyllabic verbs' (examples wandika 'they are coming', análima 'he is hoeing', nábwēni 'I saw him', anapyajila, wanajōmboka), apparently on the tense/subject prefix; the full sentence is not recoverable from the snippets.
new_statements.exceptions: (i) Enclitic suffixes -pe and -ga/-je do not always attract stress: a long stressed syllable keeps it (kundáwipe, ajéndeje); (ii) trisyllabic verbs have antepenultimate stress in their simple forms but penultimate stress with conjugational endings (kukágula 'to follow'); (iii) monosyllabic words (few, mostly ideophones) have ultimate stress; (iv) trisyllabic ideophones stress the first syllable (p. 125); (v) p. 58: after possessive contraction 'the stress is then shifted onto the penultimate syllable'. Harries adds (p. 16) that tone 'is not such an important feature of Mwera as length of vowels' (three level tones); Odden 1999/2003 analyse Mwera as a P-zone tone language with grammatical (non-lexical) verbal H tones.
new_statements.domain_note: Word domain: 'Each word in Mwera has one main stress' (p. 15) and 'Every Mwera word contains a main stress, and only one main stress' (p. 17, used as the criterion for word division). Stress described as co-occurring with penultimate length and rising tone, i.e. the Eastern Bantu penultimate-prominence pattern; no separate phrase-level statement was visible in the snippets. Access was via Google Books search-inside snippets of the 1950 print (two scans give identical text); the full page was not viewable.
new_statements.identity_note: Harries 1950 describes 'Mwera' of the south-eastern Tanganyika Territory (Lindi area) = Glottolog mwer1248 (P22), the same variety Taji & Mreta 2017 call Shimwela and Odden 1999 calls Mwera (data from a UDSM speaker, 1997). Not to be confused with the 'Mbamba Bay Mwera' (N201, Lake Nyasa), a different language listed separately in Maho's update of Guthrie.

sources.note: Sec. 2.3: 'All P-zone languages are tonal'; contour tones restricted to heavy syllables/long vowels/VN in Yao and Mwera; vowel length preserved in Yao-Mwera; predictable (tense-determined) verbal tone across zone P. Nothing specific about Mwera stress or penultimate lengthening (PL discussed only for Makonde).
